summary: Specifies how to describe BFCP streams in SDP, which user agents use in offers and answers when setting up the streams. It was standards-track and has been replaced by RFC 8856.

eli5.summary: This is the part of the call setup card that says there will also be a floor control channel, and how to reach it.

subtitle: Describes how to advertise Binary Floor Control Protocol streams in SDP offers and answers.

tldr.problem: When establishing conference calls with floor control (managing who can speak), endpoints need a way to negotiate BFCP streams in SDP offer/answer exchanges, including transport addresses and role determination.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines new SDP media lines and attributes for BFCP: TCP/BFCP and TCP/TLS/BFCP transport protocols, and attributes like 'floorctrl' to state roles, 'confid' and 'userid' for identifiers, and 'floorid' to map floors to media streams.
tldr.outcome: Endpoints can now negotiate floor control in multimedia sessions, but this was superseded by RFC 8856 with updates.

today: RFC 4583 was a Proposed Standard published in November 2006 and was obsoleted by RFC 8856. BFCP remains in use in multimedia conferencing systems that require floor control.

sections.title: Overview and Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 4583 specifies how to describe Binary Floor Control Protocol (BFCP) streams in Session Description Protocol (SDP) descriptions. BFCP is a protocol for managing who has the right to communicate (the floor) in a multimedia conference. Participants use the offer/answer model with SDP to negotiate the parameters needed to establish BFCP connections.

In a typical conference, a floor control server coordinates floor grants and requests. A BFCP client contacts the server to request or release the floor. The SDP description must convey the transport address of the floor control server, the conference identifier, the user identifier, and the role each party will play (client, server, or both).
sections.eli5: In a big video call, one person or machine decides who gets to talk. This document says how to tell everyone in the call: where the referee is, who you are, what conference you are in, and whether you will be talking or refereeing.

sections.title: SDP Media Lines and Attributes
sections.content:
BFCP is advertised using an SDP 'm' line with media type "application" and two new transport protocol values: "TCP/BFCP" for unencrypted BFCP and "TCP/TLS/BFCP" for BFCP running over TLS. The port field follows the standard SDP rules; it contains the port where the floor control server (or the endpoint initiating the connection) listens.

Several SDP attributes define the BFCP stream. The floorctrl attribute lists the roles the endpoint is willing to perform: "c-only" (client only), "s-only" (server only), or "c-s" (both roles). The offerer lists all roles it would accept; the answerer selects one. The confid and userid attributes carry integer identifiers for the conference and the user. The floorid attribute defines a floor identifier and optionally associates it with one or more media streams (audio, video) using the "mstrm" option and a reference to an SDP label attribute.
sections.eli5: The invitation says "I am ready to talk over this address, using this method" (TCP or secure TCP). It also says "I can be the referee or the talker, here is my name and ID in the meeting, and here is which call floors go with which audio or video streams."

sections.title: Role Determination and TCP Management
sections.content:
In simple scenarios, the offerer is a floor control client and the answerer is a floor control server, requiring no explicit negotiation. However, endpoints may support multiple roles. When the offerer includes a floorctrl attribute, the answerer MUST include one in the answer, choosing a single role from the offerer's list. A table in the RFC defines the complementary roles: if the offerer offers "c-only", the answerer chooses "s-only"; if the offerer offers "c-s", the answerer can choose "c-s".

TCP connection management uses two SDP attributes: setup indicates which party initiates the TCP connection (active, passive, or actpass), and connection handles reestablishment. When a TCP connection fails or is reset, the entity detecting the failure generates a new offer to reestablish the connection.
sections.eli5: The people decide who will be the talker and who the referee. They also agree on who dials whom on the phone, and what to do if the call drops.

sections.title: Authentication and TLS
sections.content:
BFCP relies on an initial integrity-protected channel to exchange self-signed certificates between the client and the floor control server. When SDP is carried in SIP, S/MIME provides this protected channel. Endpoints exchange certificate fingerprints in the SDP offer/answer exchange. The fingerprint attribute carries the hash of the certificate, allowing endpoints to verify the certificate presented during TLS handshake.

When TLS is used, once the TCP connection is established, the answerer acts as the TLS server regardless of whether it actively or passively established the TCP connection. This ensures a clear TLS role assignment. Endpoints follow rules for certificate validation: a certificate must be directly signed by one of the trust anchors or validated through a certification path ending at a trust anchor, or a fingerprint must be exchanged and verified.
sections.eli5: Before the video call really starts, the two sides swap secret fingerprints so they know it is really each other when they connect. When they connect with encryption, the person who answers the phone is always the one checking the certificate.
